                                          PROJECT NO. 58000

    RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                                §          PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                            §
    TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY                          §
    IN THE ERCOT REGION                                 §                     OF TEXAS


                      COMMENTS OF THE DATA CENTER COALITION



    I.​   INTRODUCTION

        The Data Center Coalition (DCC) is the national membership association1 for the U.S.
data center industry, representing leading data center owners and operators who maintain data
center infrastructure across the country and globe, as well as companies that lease large amounts
of data center capacity. DCC empowers and champions the data center community through
public policy advocacy, thought leadership, stakeholder outreach, and community engagement. A
vast majority of DCC member companies have teams, operations, and infrastructure in the Lone
Star State, including 13 companies headquartered in Texas.

        DCC members are committed to paying their full cost of service and to providing
financial assurances that reflect the genuine risks associated with large load interconnection.
DCC's comments below are offered in that spirit: DCC supports a minimum billing demand and
transmission cost recovery framework that is properly calibrated to recover the costs large load
customers actually cause, backed by financial security and payment obligations commensurate
with the risk large loads present to the transmission system, and applied consistently and without
cross-subsidization among customer classes or between large load customers themselves.

          Like all customers, the data center industry depends on reliable electricity service to
fulfill its role as a vital backbone of the modern economy. In turn, data centers offer numerous
reliability benefits to the grid, including significant investments in new energy resources and
next-generation technologies. DCC appreciates the Electric Reliability Council of Texas's
(ERCOT) role and commitment to ensuring grid reliability for Texas homes and businesses.




1
  The Data Center Coalition is a membership organization of leading data center owners and operators. Public
testimony and written comments submitted by DCC do not necessarily reflect the views of each individual DCC
member. A list of current DCC Members is accessible at https://www.datacentercoalition.org/members.
  II.​   RESPONSES TO COMMISSION STAFF’S QUESTIONS FOR COMMENT

Question 1: Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand
provisions be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or
different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

         DCC supports an appropriately calibrated minimum billing demand that is focused on
recovering the cost of transmission capacity reserved for large load customers, consistent with
cost-causation principles. DCC does not, however, support establishing differentiated minimum
billing demand values or methodologies based solely on the magnitude of a large load customer's
contracted peak demand or NCP demand. The minimum billing demand is intended to recover
the cost of the transmission infrastructure needed to serve a particular customer. Contracted peak
demand already reflects a customer's long-term reservation of transmission capacity, so there is
no cost-based justification for applying a different value or methodology depending on how large
or small a given customer's demand happens to be. A single, consistent methodology applicable
to all large load customers also best supports the requirement that rates be just and reasonable
and not preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory. Introducing multiple customer-specific
methodologies based on size would reduce regulatory certainty for both customers and
transmission providers while providing little additional accuracy in cost recovery.


Question 2: Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
          -​ fixed for 20 years as proposed;
          -​ reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or
          -​ extended to a longer time period?®

        DCC recommends that the Commission replace the prescribed 100 percent, 20-year
minimum billing demand requirement with a data-driven, economically justified framework that
ensures TSPs and DSPs fully recover their transmission cost of service, prevents cost shifting to
other customer classes, and does not recover more than the cost of the investment made to serve
large load customers. That framework should apply for a term shorter than the 20 years currently
proposed, and at a level below the fixed, full-level obligation currently proposed for that entire
term. The purpose of the minimum billing demand, like the 12CP methodology itself, is to
ensure accurate recovery of the transmission cost of service, not to generate collections beyond
what is needed to recover the cost of the investment made to serve the large load customer.

       Cost recovery should be the touchstone the Commission applies in setting this
requirement, and the term and percentage associated with the minimum billing demand should be
appropriately sized to ensure timely cost recovery. A 20-year, 100 percent minimum billing
demand is too long and high to serve that purpose. The record in this proceeding already
demonstrates that lower percentages and shorter terms are workable: the Texas Energy Buyers
 Alliance (TEBA) submitted an independently commissioned study modeling minimum billing
demand levels ranging from 60 to 100 percent of contracted demand, and a range of
corresponding obligation periods, against approximately 53 gigawatts of projected new
large-load growth and approximately $37 billion in transmission investment.2 That study found
that a minimum billing demand of 75 percent of contracted demand for approximately 13 years,
or 80 percent for approximately 9 years, fully recovers the transmission cost of service
attributable to new large loads and holds existing customers harmless. Accordingly, DCC
recommends that the Commission adopt one of these approaches uniformly for all large load
customers, rather than the proposed 100 percent, 20-year requirement or an approach that varies
on a customer-by-customer or project-by-project basis.

        DCC has not identified another jurisdiction that has set a minimum billing demand at the
full 100 percent of contracted demand; the highest level DCC is aware of is 90 percent. Nor has
DCC identified another jurisdiction that pairs a 20-year minimum term with a minimum billing
demand anywhere near that level. DCC raises this simply to help inform where the proposed
requirement sits relative to comparable approaches elsewhere, and remains ready to work with
the Commission and Staff to identify a level and term that reflects Texas's specific transmission
investment needs.

        DCC further recommends that the minimum billing demand apply only to the
transmission capacity made available to the large load customer. For large load customers subject
to the phased energization schedules required under §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load
Interconnection Standards), DCC recommends that the Commission clarify that "available
service" refers to the transmission capacity that has been constructed, tested, and made available
under the applicable phase of the customer's interconnection agreement, consistent with DCC's
response to Question 6. Where a utility fails to make capacity available on the agreed schedule,
or delivery is delayed by a force majeure event, the minimum billing demand should be adjusted
accordingly so that a large load customer is not billed for capacity it has not actually been made
able to use. Tying the minimum billing demand to available capacity, rather than to the full
contracted level irrespective of energization status, keeps the obligation consistent with the cost
recovery rationale described above: the customer pays for what the system has made available to
serve it, and no more.

        Any such framework should remain subject to true-up and reconciliation to ensure that
TSPs and DSPs continue to fully recover their approved transmission cost of service and that
other customer classes are held harmless from any resulting shortfall. That analysis should
expressly consider transmission asset depreciation, expected utilization, customer financial
security already provided under §25.194, and projected customer retention over the recovery
period. The framework should not reduce or delay the financial security and

2
 Comments of the Texas Energy Buyers Alliance, Project No. 58000, Item No. 12 (filed July 30, 2026),
https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/search/documents/?controlNumber=58000&itemNumber=12.
 contribution-in-aid-of-construction obligations that apply to large load customers under §25.194
of this title. Given the significant overlap between this rulemaking and Project No. 58481,
Rulemaking to Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards Under PURA §37.0561,
including shared definitions and cross-references for contracted peak demand, financial security,
and interconnection fees, DCC asks the Commission to clarify how the minimum billing demand
recovered under this rulemaking interacts with interconnection fees and forfeited financial
security collected under §25.194, which subsection (k) of this section already requires TSPs to
apply as an offset to the transmission revenue requirement, so that the requirements adopted here
remain consistent with, and not duplicative of, the standards adopted in that proceeding, and
large load customers are not charged twice for the same underlying investment through separate
mechanisms in the two rulemakings.

       The Commission should ensure that minimum billing demand,
contribution-in-aid-of-construction, financial security, direct interconnection charges, and
transmission rates operate as complementary mechanisms rather than cumulative mechanisms
recovering the same underlying transmission investment. Any amounts recovered through one
mechanism should be transparently reflected in the utility's transmission revenue requirement to
prevent duplicate recovery while ensuring full recovery of prudent costs.


Question 3: Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of
demand lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the
large load minimum billing demand:
           -​ reflect a “ratcheted” demand, wherein the large load minimum billing
              demand is some percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or
              maximum NCP demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet
              percentage decline in phases over the years, and how?
           -​ be based on a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, wherein the
              large load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large
              load customer’s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the
              previous year and the large load customer’s 12CP demand? If so, should the
              percentage weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand
              decline in phases over the years, and how?

        Consistent with DCC's recommendation in response to Question 2, DCC recommends
that the Commission adopt a data-driven, economically justified framework for the minimum
billing demand that ensures TSPs and DSPs fully recover their transmission cost of service,
prevents cost shifting to other customer classes, and does not recover more than the cost of the
investment made to serve large load customers. Between the two approaches presented, DCC
supports a ratcheted minimum billing demand, set as a percentage of the large load customer's
contracted peak demand, consistent with the phased treatment of available capacity described in
 DCC's responses to Questions 2 and 6, over a weighted-average approach. DCC's preference
reflects the value of a stable, consistently applied basis for calculating the minimum billing
demand, rather than a preference for any particular mechanism. A weighted-average approach
would require recalculating the customer's 12CP demand annually and could involve shifting
weightings over time, adding complexity for TSPs and DSPs to administer consistently.

        DCC recommends that the Commission adopt a minimum billing demand within the
range described in DCC's response to Question 2: 75 percent of contracted demand for
approximately 13 years, or 80 percent for approximately 9 years, and that the percentage not
exceed approximately 85 percent of contracted demand. The independently commissioned study
described in DCC's response to Question 2 demonstrates that a percentage within this range,
combined with an appropriately calibrated term, fully recovers the transmission cost of service
attributable to new large loads and holds existing customers harmless, without generating
collections beyond what is needed to recover that cost.3 DCC recommends that the Commission
set the specific percentage using this type of data-driven cost of service analysis, so that the
minimum billing demand recovers no more than the cost of the investment it is intended to fund.

        Regardless of which structure the Commission adopts, DCC recommends that the
minimum billing demand fully recover the transmission cost of service attributable to the large
load customer, without resulting in cross-subsidization, whether by other customer classes on
behalf of large load customers or among large load customers themselves. If the Commission
adopts a minimum billing demand term longer than what DCC recommends in response to
Question 2, DCC recommends that the Commission apply a ratchet to reduce the percentage over
the remainder of the term, so that the minimum billing demand continues to decline as the
associated transmission investment is depreciated and recovered.



Question 4: Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load,
defined as an entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load
Interconnection Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists
of power electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and
cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include applicable
legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large computational
loads.

       DCC recommends that the Commission decline to adopt separate rate treatment for large
computational load as defined in this question. Any requirements applicable to large loads should
be based on the existing 75 MW threshold that already defines a large load customer under

3
    Comments of the Texas Energy Buyers Alliance, supra note 1.
 PURA §37.0561 and §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards), not
on a separate classification by load type. A single, size-based threshold, already established and
in use elsewhere in this rulemaking, provides a clear and consistent line; a further
sub-classification based on hardware composition does not.

        Data center load supports accurate cost allocation under the 12CP methodology. Data
center load typically operates at a high, predictable load factor relative to its contracted capacity.
This profile means a data center's billed demand under the 12CP methodology closely tracks its
actual, ongoing draw on the transmission system. Combined with the appropriately calibrated
minimum billing demand described in DCC's responses to Questions 1 through 3, this ensures
that data center load pays its full, genuine share of the transmission investment made to serve it.
The relevant inquiry for rate design is how a customer uses the transmission system, not the type
of equipment installed behind the meter.

         When large loads pay their fair share, growth can benefit rather than burden existing
customers. Several utilities have reported or projected outcomes consistent with this dynamic. A
2025 study by researchers at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that, over the
preceding five years, states with the highest load growth generally experienced declining retail
electricity prices in real terms, as fixed system costs were spread across a larger paying load
base.4 CenterPoint Energy projected in August 2026 that its planned addition of up to 14
gigawatts of new large-load projects, including data centers, would save Texas electric customers
more than $5 billion over the next decade as those loads pay a larger share of fixed grid costs.5
Indiana Michigan Power similarly announced in February 2026 that growth in revenue from
large customers, including data centers, would support a base rate reduction, and has committed
to filing the rate case with the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission to implement it, though
that proceeding remains pending.6 These outcomes reflect what a properly calibrated minimum
billing demand is designed to achieve here: large load growth that strengthens the system for all
customers.

        Rate design should be based on grid impact (measurable differences in cost causation and
use of the transmission system), rather than the industry, end use, technology, or equipment
installed behind the meter. A hardware-composition threshold is not a reasonable proxy for
transmission cost responsibility because it does not measure how a customer uses the grid or the
transmission investment required to serve that customer. The proposed definition of large
computational load, based solely on whether 50 percent or more of the demand at a site consists
4

5
  CenterPoint Energy Announces Historic "Customer Savings Initiative" Projecting $5 Billion in Affordability

6
  I&M Announces Base Rate Reduction for Hoosiers Through Customer Benefits Plan, Indiana Michigan Power
(Feb. 24, 2026), https://www.indianamichiganpower.com/company/news/view?releaseID=10776.
 of power electronic-based load, measures hardware composition, not cost causation, load factor,
or actual grid impact. It groups together loads with materially different operating profiles,
including continuously operating data centers and more flexible cryptocurrency mining
operations, based on a shared technical characteristic that does not correlate with either group's
contribution to transmission cost of service. PURA §36.001 authorizes the Commission to adopt
rules determining the classification of customers and services and the applicability of rates, but
PURA §36.003 requires that rates be just and reasonable, sufficient, equitable, and consistent in
application to each class of consumer, and not unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or
discriminatory. A rate classification must be grounded in genuine differences in cost causation to
satisfy that standard, and a hardware-composition threshold that groups together loads with
materially different operating profiles would be difficult to reconcile with that requirement. For
example, some computational loads operate as continuous, high-load-factor facilities with
predictable demand, while others may have materially different operating characteristics,
flexibility, or utilization patterns. A single rate classification based solely on the presence of
power-electronic equipment does not distinguish among these differences and therefore is not
reasonably tailored to differences in transmission cost causation.

        DCC's members have engaged constructively with Staff and other stakeholders
throughout this proceeding, including by recommending the data-driven minimum billing
demand framework described in DCC's responses to Questions 1 through 3, because DCC
recognizes the legitimate cost-recovery and reliability concerns this rulemaking is intended to
address. The 12CP methodology and minimum billing demand framework, properly calibrated,
already accomplish those objectives for all large loads. DCC recommends that the Commission
rely on that framework, applied uniformly, rather than adopt separate rate treatment for large
computational loads.



Question 5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to
include transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to
serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

        DCC recommends that the Commission not broaden the definition of transmission
interconnection costs. Whether a batch-study-recommended project should be treated as an
interconnection cost, billed directly to the requesting customer, or as a general transmission cost
of service, recovered through the network transmission service rate, should turn on what the
upgrade is intended to serve and who benefits from it. This distinction reflects longstanding
cost-causation principles that assign directly attributable facilities to individual customers while
recovering network facilities through generally applicable transmission rates. A project that
provides capacity for the exclusive use of the interconnecting load functions as a dedicated
interconnection facility and is appropriately billed to that customer. A project that provides
 capacity usable by other loads or generators on the system provides a broader benefit and should
remain part of the general transmission cost of service, consistent with how the Commission
treats other transmission investment under this section. A definition based on this distinction,
rather than on the mere fact that a project was identified through a batch study, gives the
Commission and TSPs a clear and administrable basis for classification and avoids disputes over
cost allocation that could otherwise delay large load interconnection.

         DCC further recommends that the Commission adopt a cost-sharing mechanism to
address facilities whose use changes over time. A facility classified as a customer-specific
interconnection cost at the time it is built may later be utilized to serve additional customers,
whether through subsequent interconnections or system reconfiguration. Absent a mechanism to
revisit that allocation, the original customer would bear the full cost of a facility that has come to
provide broader system benefit, on a permanent basis, even though the facility no longer serves
that customer exclusively. The Commission should require that costs be reallocated, and the
original customer credited or reimbursed accordingly, when a customer-specific facility is
subsequently used to serve others, so that the exclusive-use classification described above
remains accurate over the life of the facility rather than only at the time of initial construction.
The Commission should direct ERCOT and the transmission service providers to establish an
administratively straightforward true-up process for reallocating those costs when subsequent
customers begin using the facility. DCC also recommends a related, voluntary capacity
reallocation mechanism, described in DCC's response to Question 6.


Question 6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of
whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, how
should these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments and
transmission planning studies?

       DCC recommends that the Commission clarify that, for large load customers subject to
the phased energization schedules required under §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load
Interconnection Standards), "available service" refers to the transmission capacity that has been
constructed, tested, and made available under the applicable phase of the customer's
interconnection agreement. This approach improves both transmission planning accuracy and
resource adequacy forecasting by aligning planning assumptions with actual project development
milestones. DCC recommends this same clarification in response to Question 2, so that billing,
transmission planning, and resource adequacy assessments all reflect a single, consistent
standard tied to the staged delivery of capacity contemplated by the approved interconnection
agreement, rather than developing inconsistent, unclarified interpretations across this rulemaking
and Project No. 58481.
          Applying that standard, DCC recommends that the Commission direct ERCOT to use the
§25.194 phased energization schedule, rather than treating reserved capacity as either fully
speculative or fully available, across both long-term transmission planning and near-term
resource adequacy assessments and operational demand forecasting. For long-term transmission
planning, which requires long lead times, this means reflecting reserved capacity as each phase
of a customer's interconnection agreement is constructed and tested, so that the system is built to
serve load growth that is already financially committed under the payment and security
obligations described in §25.194 and DCC's response to Question 2. For resource adequacy
assessments and operational forecasting, the same phased schedule ensures that near-term
reliability metrics reflect the expected timing of actual load growth rather than contractual
commitments that have not yet materialized as grid draw.

        DCC recommends that the Commission clarify that a large load customer that remains
current on its minimum billing demand and other obligations under §25.194 retains its reserved
transmission capacity, rather than facing reallocation under §25.252(d)(2) of this title. DCC's
members generally prefer to meet their full payment obligations in exchange for certainty over
their reserved capacity, rather than bear the risk of losing that capacity to reallocation. A
framework that allows a paying, compliant customer to lose its reserved capacity undermines the
predictability that both the customer and the transmission system need to plan effectively.
Maintaining reservation rights for customers that remain financially compliant preserves
investment certainty while avoiding unnecessary restudies and repeated transmission planning
exercises.

        Separately, DCC recommends that the Commission establish a mechanism allowing a
large load customer to voluntarily reallocate reserved transmission capacity it does not intend to
use, with a corresponding reduction in that customer's minimum billing demand. This
mechanism is distinct from, and should not be confused with, the involuntary reallocation
addressed in the preceding paragraph. It would operate solely at the customer's election, for
customers who do not require, or are unable to use, their full reserved capacity. Upon a voluntary
reallocation, financial responsibility for the reallocated capacity, including any associated
minimum billing demand, should transfer to the customer that takes on that capacity, so that the
transmission cost of service continues to be fully recovered and no shortfall is shifted to other
customer classes. A voluntary mechanism of this kind supports efficient use of the transmission
system and rewards responsible planning by large load customers, without altering the protection
against involuntary reallocation described above.



III.​   CONCLUSION

       DCC members support a transmission cost recovery framework that ensures utilities
recover prudent transmission investments, protects existing customers from cost shifting, and
 preserves the regulatory certainty necessary to support continued investment in large-load
development across Texas. Those objectives are complementary, not competing, when rates
remain grounded in cost causation and avoid duplicate recovery.

         Data centers are critical to the modern economy and daily life, and the data center
industry is eager to contribute to solutions that ensure reliable, affordable, and adequate power
for all consumers. DCC is committed to being a collaborative partner and part of the solution to
meeting Texas's energy demand and reliability goals, and looks forward to continued engagement
with the Commission, utilities, customers, and other stakeholders across Texas.


                                                    Respectfully submitted,

​                                                   Cameron Poursoltan
​                                                   Data Center Coalition

   customer to voluntarily reallocate reserved transmission capacity it does not intend to
   use, with a corresponding reduction in that customer's minimum billing demand and a
   transfer of responsibility to the customer that takes on the capacity.
●​ DCC recommends that ERCOT use the phased energization schedule required under
   §25.194 in both long-term transmission planning and resource adequacy assessments,

●​ DCC recommends that a large load customer that remains current on its minimum billing
   demand and other §25.194 obligations retain its reserved transmission capacity and not

customers, rather than the proposed 100 percent, 20-year requirement or an approach that varies
on a customer-by-customer or proj ect-by-proj ect basis.

        DCC has not identified another jurisdiction that has set a minimum billing demand at the
full 100 percent of contracted demand; the highest level DCC is aware of is 90 percent. Nor has
DCC identified another jurisdiction that pairs a 20-year minimum term with a minimum billing
demand anywhere near that level. DCC raises this simply to help inform where the proposed
requirement sits relative to comparable approaches elsewhere, and remains ready to work with
the Commission and Staff to identify a level and term that reflects Texas's specific transmission
investment needs.

         DCC further recommends that the minimum billing demand apply only to the
transmission capacity made available to the large load customer. For large load customers subject
to the phased energization schedules required under §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load
Interconnection Standards), DCC recommends that the Commission clarify that "available
service" refers to the transmission capacity that has been constructed, tested, and made available
under the applicable phase of the customer's interconnection agreement, consistent with DCC's
response to Question 6. Where a utility fails to make capacity available on the agreed schedule,
or delivery is delayed by a force majeure event, the minimum billing demand should be adjusted
accordingly so that a large load customer is not billed for capacity it has not actually been made
able to use. Tying the minimum billing demand to available capacity, rather than to the full
contracted level irrespective of energization status, keeps the obligation consistent with the cost
recovery rationale described above: the customer pays for what the system has made available to
serve it, and no more.

        Any such framework should remain subj ect to true-up and reconciliation to ensure that
TSPs and DSPs continue to fully recover their approved transmission cost of service and that
other customer classes are held harmless from any resulting shortfall. That analysis should
expressly consider transmission asset depreciation, expected utilization, customer financial
security already provided under §25.194, and proj ected customer retention over the recovery
period. The framework should not reduce or delay the financial security and

of this title. Given the significant overlap between this rulemaking and Project No. 58481,

mechanisms in the two rulemakings.

       The Commission should ensure that minimum billing demand,
contribution-in-aid-of-construction, financial security, direct interconnection charges, and
transmission rates operate as complementary mechanisms rather than cumulative mechanisms
recovering the same underlying transmission investment. Any amounts recovered through one
mechanism should be transparently reflected in the utility's transmission revenue requirement to
prevent duplicate recovery while ensuring full recovery of prudent costs.


Question 3: Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of
demand lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the
large load minimum billing demand:
           - reflect a "ratcheted" demand, wherein the large load minimum billing
              demand is some percentage of the customer's contracted peak demand or
              maximum NCP demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet
              percentage decline in phases over the years, and how?
           - be based on a "weighted average" minimum billing demand, wherein the
              large load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large
              load customer's contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the
              previous year and the large load customer's 12CP demand? If so, should the
              percentage weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand
              decline in phases over the years, and how?

        Consistent with DCC's recommendation in response to Question 2, DCC recommends
that the Commission adopt a data-driven, economically justified framework for the minimum
billing demand that ensures TSPs and DSPs fully recover their transmission cost of service,
prevents cost shifting to other customer classes, and does not recover more than the cost of the
investment made to serve large load customers. Between the two approaches presented, DCC
supports a ratcheted minimum billing demand, set as a percentage of the large load customer's
contracted peak demand, consistent with the phased treatment of available capacity described in
 DCC's responses to Questions 2 and 6, over a weighted-average approach. DCC's preference
reflects the value of a stable, consistently applied basis for calculating the minimum billing
demand, rather than a preference for any particular mechanism. A weighted-average approach
would require recalculating the customer's 12CP demand annually and could involve shifting
weightings over time, adding complexity for TSPs and DSPs to administer consistently.

        DCC recommends that the Commission adopt a minimum billing demand within the
range described in DCC's response to Question 2: 75 percent of contracted demand for
approximately 13 years, or 80 percent for approximately 9 years, and that the percentage not
exceed approximately 85 percent of contracted demand. The independently commissioned study
described in DCC's response to Question 2 demonstrates that a percentage within this range,
combined with an appropriately calibrated term, fully recovers the transmission cost of service
attributable to new large loads and holds existing customers harmless, without generating
collections beyond what is needed to recover that cost.3 DCC recommends that the Commission
set the specific percentage using this type of data-driven cost of service analysis, so that the
minimum billing demand recovers no more than the cost of the investment it is intended to fund.

       Regardless of which structure the Commission adopts, DCC recommends that the
minimum billing demand fully recover the transmission cost of service attributable to the large
load customer, without resulting in cross-subsidization, whether by other customer classes on
behalf of large load customers or among large load customers themselves. If the Commission
adopts a minimum billing demand term longer than what DCC recommends in response to
Question 2, DCC recommends that the Commission apply a ratchet to reduce the percentage over
the remainder of the term, so that the minimum billing demand continues to decline as the
associated transmission investment is depreciated and recovered.



Question 4: Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load,
defined as an entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load
Interconnection Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists
of power electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and
cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include applicable
legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large computational
loads.

       DCC recommends that the Commission decline to adopt separate rate treatment for large
computational load as defined in this question. Any requirements applicable to large loads should
be based on the existing 75 MW threshold that already defines a large load customer under


3 Comments of the Texas Energy Buyers Alliance, supra note 1.
 PURA §37.0561 and §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards), not
on a separate classification by load type. A single, size-based threshold, already established and
in use elsewhere in this rulemaking, provides a clear and consistent line; a further
sub-classification based on hardware composition does not.

         Data center load supports accurate cost allocation under the 12CP methodology. Data
center load typically operates at a high, predictable load factor relative to its contracted capacity.
This profile means a data center's billed demand under the 12CP methodology closely tracks its
actual, ongoing draw on the transmission system. Combined with the appropriately calibrated
minimum billing demand described in DCC's responses to Questions 1 through 3, this ensures
that data center load pays its full, genuine share of the transmission investment made to serve it.
The relevant inquiry for rate design is how a customer uses the transmission system, not the type
of equipment installed behind the meter.

         When large loads pay their fair share, growth can benefit rather than burden existing
customers. Several utilities have reported or projected outcomes consistent with this dynamic. A
2025 study by researchers at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that, over the
preceding five years, states with the highest load growth generally experienced declining retail
electricity prices in real terms, as fixed system costs were spread across a larger paying load
base.4 CenterPoint Energy projected in August 2026 that its planned addition of up to 14
gigawatts of new large-load proj ects, including data centers, would save Texas electric customers
more than $5 billion over the next decade as those loads pay a larger share of fixed grid costs.5
Indiana Michigan Power similarly announced in February 2026 that growth in revenue from
large customers, including data centers, would support a base rate reduction, and has committed
to filing the rate case with the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission to implement it, though
that proceeding remains pending.6 These outcomes reflect what a properly calibrated minimum
billing demand is designed to achieve here: large load growth that strengthens the system for all
customers.

         Rate design should be based on grid impact (measurable differences in cost causation and
use of the transmission system), rather than the industry, end use, technology, or equipment
installed behind the meter. A hardware-composition threshold is not a reasonable proxy for
transmission cost responsibility because it does not measure how a customer uses the grid or the
transmission investment required to serve that customer. The proposed definition of large
computational load, based solely on whether 50 percent or more of the demand at a site consists

or actual grid impact. It groups together loads with materially different operating profiles,
including continuously operating data centers and more flexible cryptocurrency mining
operations, based on a shared technical characteristic that does not correlate with either group's
contribution to transmission cost of service. PURA §36.001 authorizes the Commission to adopt
rules determining the classification of customers and services and the applicability of rates, but
PURA §36.003 requires that rates be just and reasonable, sufficient, equitable, and consistent in
application to each class of consumer, and not unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or
discriminatory. A rate classification must be grounded in genuine differences in cost causation to
satisfy that standard, and a hardware-composition threshold that groups together loads with
materially different operating profiles would be difficult to reconcile with that requirement. For
example, some computational loads operate as continuous, high-load-factor facilities with
predictable demand, while others may have materially different operating characteristics,
flexibility, or utilization patterns. A single rate classification based solely on the presence of
power-electronic equipment does not distinguish among these differences and therefore is not
reasonably tailored to differences in transmission cost causation.

        DCC's members have engaged constructively with Staff and other stakeholders
throughout this proceeding, including by recommending the data-driven minimum billing
demand framework described in DCC's responses to Questions 1 through 3, because DCC
recognizes the legitimate cost-recovery and reliability concerns this rulemaking is intended to
address. The 12CP methodology and minimum billing demand framework, properly calibrated,
already accomplish those objectives for alllarge loads. DCC recommends that the Commission
rely on that framework, applied uniformly, rather than adopt separate rate treatment for large
computational loads.



Question 5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to
include transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to
serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

        DCC recommends that the Commission not broaden the definition of transmission
interconnection costs. Whether a batch-study-recommended proj ect should be treated as an
interconnection cost, billed directly to the requesting customer, or as a general transmission cost
of service, recovered through the network transmission service rate, should turn on what the
upgrade is intended to serve and who benefits from it. This distinction reflects longstanding
cost-causation principles that assign directly attributable facilities to individual customers while
recovering network facilities through generally applicable transmission rates. A project that
provides capacity for the exclusive use of the interconnecting load functions as a dedicated
interconnection facility and is appropriately billed to that customer. A project that provides
 capacity usable by other loads or generators on the system provides a broader benefit and should
remain part of the general transmission cost of service, consistent with how the Commission
treats other transmission investment under this section. A definition based on this distinction,
rather than on the mere fact that a project was identified through a batch study, gives the
Commission and TSPs a clear and administrable basis for classification and avoids disputes over
cost allocation that could otherwise delay large load interconnection.

         DCC further recommends that the Commission adopt a cost-sharing mechanism to
address facilities whose use changes over time. A facility classified as a customer-specific
interconnection cost at the time it is built may later be utilized to serve additional customers,
whether through subsequent interconnections or system reconfiguration. Absent a mechanism to
revisit that allocation, the original customer would bear the full cost of a facility that has come to
provide broader system benefit, on a permanent basis, even though the facility no longer serves
that customer exclusively. The Commission should require that costs be reallocated, and the
original customer credited or reimbursed accordingly, when a customer-specific facility is
subsequently used to serve others, so that the exclusive-use classification described above
remains accurate over the life of the facility rather than only at the time of initial construction.
The Commission should direct ERCOT and the transmission service providers to establish an
administratively straightforward true-up process for reallocating those costs when subsequent
customers begin using the facility. DCC also recommends a related, voluntary capacity
reallocation mechanism, described in DCC's response to Question 6.


Question 6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of
whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, how
should these loads be rellected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments and
transmission planning studies?

       DCC recommends that the Commission clarify that, for large load customers subject to
the phased energization schedules required under §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load
Interconnection Standards), "available service" refers to the transmission capacity that has been
constructed, tested, and made available under the applicable phase of the customer's
interconnection agreement. This approach improves both transmission planning accuracy and
resource adequacy forecasting by aligning planning assumptions with actual proj ect development
milestones. DCC recommends this same clarification in response to Question 2, so that billing,
transmission planning, and resource adequacy assessments all reflect a single, consistent
standard tied to the staged delivery of capacity contemplated by the approved interconnection
agreement, rather than developing inconsistent, unclarified interpretations across this rulemaking
and Project No. 58481.
          Applying that standard, DCC recommends that the Commission direct ERCOT to use the
§25.194 phased energization schedule, rather than treating reserved capacity as either fully
speculative or fully available, across both long-term transmission planning and near-term
resource adequacy assessments and operational demand forecasting. For long-term transmission
planning, which requires long lead times, this means reflecting reserved capacity as each phase
of a customer's interconnection agreement is constructed and tested, so that the system is built to
serve load growth that is already financially committed under the payment and security
obligations described in §25.194 and DCC's response to Question 2. For resource adequacy
assessments and operational forecasting, the same phased schedule ensures that near-term
reliability metrics reflect the expected timing of actual load growth rather than contractual
commitments that have not yet materialized as grid draw.

       DCC recommends that the Commission clarify that a large load customer that remains
current on its minimum billing demand and other obligations under §25.194 retains its reserved
transmission capacity, rather than facing reallocation under §25.252(d)(2) of this title. DCC's
members generally prefer to meet their full payment obligations in exchange for certainty over
their reserved capacity, rather than bear the risk of losing that capacity to reallocation. A
framework that allows a paying, compliant customer to lose its reserved capacity undermines the
predictability that both the customer and the transmission system need to plan effectively.
Maintaining reservation rights for customers that remain financially compliant preserves
investment certainty while avoiding unnecessary restudies and repeated transmission planning
exercises.

        Separately, DCC recommends that the Commission establish a mechanism allowing a
large load customer to voluntarily reallocate reserved transmission capacity it does not intend to
use, with a corresponding reduction in that customer's minimum billing demand. This
mechanism is distinct from, and should not be confused with, the involuntary reallocation
addressed in the preceding paragraph. It would operate solely at the customer's election, for
customers who do not require, or are unable to use, their full reserved capacity. Upon a voluntary
reallocation, financial responsibility for the reallocated capacity, including any associated
minimum billing demand, should transfer to the customer that takes on that capacity, so that the
transmission cost of service continues to be fully recovered and no shortfall is shifted to other
customer classes. A voluntary mechanism of this kind supports efficient use of the transmission
system and rewards responsible planning by large load customers, without altering the protection
against involuntary reallocation described above.



III.   CONCLUSION

       DCC members support a transmission cost recovery framework that ensures utilities
recover prudent transmission investments, protects existing customers from cost shifting, and
 preserves the regulatory certainty necessary to support continued investment in large-load
development across Texas. Those obj ectives are complementary, not competing, when rates
remain grounded in cost causation and avoid duplicate recovery.

       Data centers are critical to the modern economy and daily life, and the data center
industry is eager to contribute to solutions that ensure reliable, affordable, and adequate power
for all consumers. DCC is committed to being a collaborative partner and part of the solution to
meeting Texas's energy demand and reliability goals, and looks forward to continued engagement
with the Commission, utilities, customers, and other stakeholders across Texas.
